title: Lantern dispatch console — choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned The Incident Log. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Incident Log
options.lineage: fire control room teleprinter roll and printed run sheet
options.thesis: The console is not a dashboard watching an incident — it IS the incident record, writing itself in real time. Every bus event prints one timestamped line into a continuous log, and the panels are attachments pinned off it. Refuses the glowing mission-control grid of equal cards.
options.viewport: A true-white printed log column runs floor to ceiling on the left over a near-black steel ground: sprocket margin, sequence numbers, timestamps, one monospace size. Transcript fragments print as they are spoken — partials in grey carbon, striking to solid black the moment they are final. Entities are not filed to a sidebar; they are stamped into the log line where they were said, in red overprint. Right of it, attachments open in dark voids: approach, agent cam, floor plan, each a pinned sheet with a header stamp, never a rounded card.
options.risk: A printed-record world has to carry photographic content — Street View, agent screenshots, a full-bleed video. If the sheets read as decoration around the photos rather than the record they are pinned to, it becomes costume.

raised.raise: Accent economy: red and hi-vis yellow appear ONLY where incident state changes — never as decoration, never as a section colour. If a colour is not reporting a fact, it comes out.
Two scales, no middle: incident-critical values (address, victim location, stage) enormous; everything else at log size. Nothing in between, so the screen ranks itself at four metres.
The phase-1 to phase-2 change is one authored transformation of the whole console, not a route swap: the panels visibly draw down and gather into the corner menu as the video takes the screen.
Regions are separated by deep dark voids, not by card chrome or borders — which kills the identical-card-grid reflex outright.

options.label: The Approach Plate
options.thesis: A plate is how you arrive somewhere you have never seen, at night, in zero visibility — which is literally this product. Plan view above, profile view below, minimums box bottom-left: the console splits the same way into approach, interior, and the go/no-go facts.
options.viewport: Dense monochrome chart on black. The building sits in a plan view with the approach vector drawn to the front door; a profile band under it carries storeys and entry level; a boxed minimums panel bottom-left holds victim, hazards, route. Every number in a ruled cell with a keyed legend.
options.risk: This is where most careful runs in this category land — a dark technical chart for an emergency tool is the obvious strong answer, and the one a judge is most likely to have seen before.

options.label: Seven-Segment Panel
options.lineage: the seven-segment family: alarm clocks, price totems, scoreboards, fire alarm panels
options.thesis: A rigid cell mask where unlit segments are designed too. Pending stages render as ghost cells, done stages ignite — nothing slides, everything swaps instantly.
options.viewport: The console as a fixed mask of cells that never reflow; stage status is a lit or ghosted row, and the unset-clock blink is the error state.
options.case: Wins audience identification outright — appliance dashboards and fire alarm panels are this exact language — and 'unlit segments are designed too' is a native answer to the hardest constraint here: every panel must render a truthful pending state without its event ever arriving. Loses product clarity: a segment mask cannot host Street View, agent screenshots or a full-bleed video without becoming a frame around photos it does not own.
options.risk: Reads as retro novelty the moment the mask bends for photographic content.

options.label: Timetable Slide Rack
options.lineage: 1971 pocket airline timetable on a lit goldenrod bed
options.thesis: One single type size for the entire console — rank carried by weight, case, reversal and rule instead of scale. Slides rake across a lit bed; state is a mark in a fixed cell.
options.viewport: One continuous raked rack of incident slides, a tick rail showing position and extent, one element per screen reversed to an opaque plate.
options.case: Holds audience identification — the printed operational timetable is a first cousin of the fire control run sheet, and its one-size discipline is genuinely how these documents work. Loses product clarity on this surface: an 11-degree rake fights a full-bleed video phase, and single-size hierarchy is a real risk on a screen judged at four metres where the room must see the critical value instantly.
options.risk: The rake becomes decoration the moment content is photographic.

options.label: Monochrome Product Marketing
options.lineage: near-black on near-white software marketing with one restrained accent
options.case: Fuses poorly: claim-and-proof topology has nothing to say about a live incident, and a dispatch operator does not identify with a product page.
options.kept: Accent economy — one accent used four times on a whole surface.

options.label: Variable Font Specimen
options.lineage: interactive type specimen with live axis sliders
options.case: Fuses poorly: an axis/glyph/size topology maps to nothing in an incident, and audience identification is zero.
options.kept: Hierarchy by scale contrast alone — enormous against tiny, no middle sizes.

options.label: Drawcord Cape
options.lineage: silk cape with hidden drawcord channels
options.case: Fuses poorly: no dispatch audience identification and no operational grammar, though one pull turning a flat plane into volume does echo floor plan into 3D.
options.kept: A single authored transformation that reorganizes the whole surface.

options.label: Cloud Quarry
options.lineage: cut blocks of weather assembled into temporary buildings
options.case: Fuses poorly on both axes: surreal construction has no claim on an emergency record and would actively undermine trust in the data.
options.kept: Sections separated by deep voids rather than borders.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: The mission-control dashboard: dark slate ground, equal glowing panels in a grid, cyan and red status pills, a map tile top-left. Executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: A grid of equal-weight cards, each with an icon header and a status chip, over a dark slate ground.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every command-centre demo the judges will see today.
